attraction.body: A clean-up step: when the recognizer confuses two sounds in a way that teaches nothing (b heard as v), the expected sound is kept. Native changes are never touched.
attraction.title: Attraction

canonical.body: The dictionary form lined up with the audio, sound by sound, so each expected sound can be compared with what was heard at the same moment.
canonical.title: Expected form, placed in time

content-word.body: A word that carries meaning: nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs. They usually keep their full vowels and get the stress.
content-word.title: Content word

dictionary-form.body: How a dictionary writes the word when it is said slowly and alone (the citation form). Written between slashes: /…/.
dictionary-form.title: Dictionary form

divergence.body: How far what was said is from the dictionary form, averaged per sound: 0 means identical.
divergence.title: Divergence

engine.body: The model that listens to the audio and writes down the sounds it hears. The default, TIMIT-61, was trained on careful phonetic transcriptions and hears taps, glottal stops and unreleased stops.
engine.title: Phone engine

f0.body: How high or low the voice is, moment by moment (the fundamental frequency). The line rises in questions and falls at the end of statements.
f0.title: Pitch (F0)

family.body: Phenomena are grouped in four families: reduction (sounds weaken), t/d processes, assimilation (sounds blend) and word boundary (words run together). Each family has its own icon and underline style.
family.title: Family of phenomena

function-word.body: A grammar word: articles, prepositions, pronouns, auxiliaries, conjunctions. They are usually unstressed and reduced.
function-word.title: Function word

intonation-unit.body: A stretch of speech with one melody, usually a sentence or a phrase. Its last pitch movement tells a statement (falls) from a yes/no question (rises).
intonation-unit.title: Intonation unit

ipa.body: The International Phonetic Alphabet: one symbol for each sound, the same in every language. It shows what spelling hides — water has a [ɾ], not a [t].
ipa.title: IPA

ipa:aɪ.body: The jaw starts wide open with the tongue low, then everything closes up to /ɪ/.
ipa:aɪ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:aɪ.title: [aɪ] closing diphthong

ipa:aɪə.body: Like “fire” but ending in a plain schwa, with no r-colouring.
ipa:aɪə.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:aɪə.title: [aɪə] triphthong

ipa:aɪɚ.body: Three targets without a pause: open, then /ɪ/, then r-coloured.
ipa:aɪɚ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:aɪɚ.title: [aɪɚ] triphthong

ipa:aʊ.body: Starts low, then the tongue pulls back and the lips round towards /ʊ/.
ipa:aʊ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:aʊ.title: [aʊ] closing diphthong

ipa:b.body: The same seal as /p/, but the vocal folds are already vibrating when it opens.
ipa:b.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:b.title: [b] voiced bilabial stop

ipa:b̚.body: The /b/ seal held shut and never opened; the voice fades away inside the closure.
ipa:b̚.example: As in: the -b of “club” before a pause
ipa:b̚.learnMoreLabel: See the change it belongs to
ipa:b̚.title: [b̚] unreleased voiced bilabial stop

ipa:d.body: The same seal as /t/, with the voice running through it.
ipa:d.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:d.title: [d] voiced alveolar stop

ipa:dʒ.body: The voiced version: closure and then /ʒ/. It is what /d/ becomes before a /j/ (“did you” → dɪdʒu).
ipa:dʒ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:dʒ.title: [dʒ] voiced postalveolar affricate

ipa:d̚.body: The /d/ seal held with no release; the voicing dies away inside the closure.
ipa:d̚.example: As in: the -d of “good” in “good times”
ipa:d̚.learnMoreLabel: See the change it belongs to
ipa:d̚.title: [d̚] unreleased voiced alveolar stop

ipa:eə.body: Mid front vowel relaxing back into schwa.
ipa:eə.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:eə.title: [eə] centring diphthong

ipa:eɪ.body: Starts near /ɛ/ and closes upwards to /ɪ/. Stopping at the start is the commonest way to make it sound foreign.
ipa:eɪ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:eɪ.title: [eɪ] closing diphthong

ipa:f.body: The lower lip touches the upper teeth and the air hisses between them. The lips never meet each other.
ipa:f.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:f.title: [f] voiceless labiodental fricative

ipa:h.body: Nothing blocks the mouth: the noise is made at the vocal folds while the tongue is already shaped for the vowel that follows.
ipa:h.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:h.title: [h] voiceless glottal fricative

ipa:i.body: The tongue is as high and as far forward as it goes without hissing; the lips are spread.
ipa:i.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:i.title: [i] close front unrounded vowel

ipa:iə.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:iə.title: [iə] centring diphthong

ipa:iː.body: The tongue is as high and as far forward as it goes without hissing; the lips are spread.
ipa:iː.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:iː.title: [i] close front unrounded vowel

ipa:j.body: The tongue starts as high and as front as an /i/ and immediately slides off it.
ipa:j.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:j.title: [j] palatal approximant

ipa:ju.body: /j/ then /u/: the tongue starts against the palate and slides back while the lips round.
ipa:ju.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:ju.title: [ju] rising diphthong

ipa:k.body: The back of the tongue rises and seals against the soft palate.
ipa:k.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:k.title: [k] voiceless velar stop

ipa:k̚.body: The back of the tongue seals against the velum and stays there; the release never comes.
ipa:k̚.example: As in: the -k of “look” in “look back”
ipa:k̚.learnMoreLabel: See the change it belongs to
ipa:k̚.title: [k̚] unreleased voiceless velar stop

ipa:l.body: The tip touches the ridge but the sides of the tongue stay clear: the air leaves around them. At the end of a syllable the back rises too — that is the “dark” l.
ipa:l.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:l.title: [l] alveolar lateral approximant

ipa:l̩.body: A dark /l/ that is the whole syllable: no vowel comes before it, the tongue goes straight to the ridge.
ipa:l̩.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:l̩.title: [l̩] syllabic alveolar lateral

ipa:m.body: Lips closed and the velum drops: the whole airstream leaves through the nose.
ipa:m.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:m.title: [m] bilabial nasal

ipa:m̩.body: An /m/ that is the whole syllable: the lips stay closed and the voice hums through the nose with no vowel before it.
ipa:m̩.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:m̩.title: [m̩] syllabic bilabial nasal

ipa:n.body: Tongue tip on the ridge and velum down: the mouth is blocked, the nose is not.
ipa:n.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:n.title: [n] alveolar nasal

ipa:n̩.body: An /n/ that carries the syllable by itself: the tongue never leaves the ridge, and there is no vowel before it. Heard in “button” [bʌʔn̩] and “didn't”.
ipa:n̩.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:n̩.title: [n̩] syllabic alveolar nasal

ipa:oɹ.body: Like “north” but starting higher; most Americans no longer keep the two apart.
ipa:oɹ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:oɹ.title: [oɹ] r-coloured vowel

ipa:oʊ.body: Starts mid-back with the lips already rounded and closes towards /ʊ/.
ipa:oʊ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:oʊ.title: [oʊ] closing diphthong

ipa:oːɹ.body: Like “north” but starting higher; most Americans no longer keep the two apart.
ipa:oːɹ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:oːɹ.title: [oɹ] r-coloured vowel

ipa:p.body: Both lips seal, the pressure builds up behind them, and the release is a puff of air.
ipa:p.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:p.title: [p] voiceless bilabial stop

ipa:p̚.body: The lips seal as for /p/ and stay sealed: no puff of air, the next sound starts from behind closed lips.
ipa:p̚.example: As in: the -p of “stop” said curtly
ipa:p̚.learnMoreLabel: See the change it belongs to
ipa:p̚.title: [p̚] unreleased voiceless bilabial stop

ipa:s.body: A narrow groove between the tip of the tongue and the ridge; the air whistles through it.
ipa:s.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:s.title: [s] voiceless alveolar fricative

ipa:t.body: The tip of the tongue seals against the ridge behind the upper teeth.
ipa:t.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:t.title: [t] voiceless alveolar stop

ipa:tʃ.body: A stop that does not open straight up: it releases into the hiss of /ʃ/.
ipa:tʃ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:tʃ.title: [tʃ] voiceless postalveolar affricate

ipa:t̚.body: The tip seals on the ridge and simply stays there: no burst. American English does this to most final /t/s — the /t/ is in the mouth, not in the ear. Listen for a tiny silence where the t should be: “that one” sounds like “tha' one”.
ipa:t̚.example: As in: the -t of “that” in “that one”
ipa:t̚.learnMoreLabel: See the change it belongs to
ipa:t̚.title: [t̚] unreleased voiceless alveolar stop

ipa:u.body: The back of the tongue rises towards the velum while the lips round and push forward.
ipa:u.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:u.title: [u] close back rounded vowel

ipa:uː.body: The back of the tongue rises towards the velum while the lips round and push forward.
ipa:uː.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:uː.title: [u] close back rounded vowel

ipa:v.body: Like /f/, with voice. Watch the lip against the teeth: a /b/ closes both lips instead. Spanish b and v are one sound; English keeps “berry” and “very” apart.
ipa:v.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:v.title: [v] voiced labiodental fricative

ipa:w.body: Two narrowings at once: the lips round hard and the back of the tongue rises towards the velum.
ipa:w.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:w.title: [w] labial-velar approximant

ipa:z.body: The same groove as /s/, with the vocal folds vibrating. Spanish has no /z/: “rise” and “rice”, “plays” and “place” differ only by it.
ipa:z.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:z.title: [z] voiced alveolar fricative

ipa:æ.body: The front of the tongue stays forward while the jaw drops wide open. It is the widest front vowel English has. Between Spanish a and e: “cat”. Saying [ɛ] or [a] instead is a common accent marker.
ipa:æ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:æ.title: [æ] near-open front unrounded vowel

ipa:ð.body: The same tongue between the teeth as /θ/, with the voice on. Not the same as [d]: “they” and “day” are different words.
ipa:ð.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:ð.title: [ð] voiced dental fricative

ipa:ŋ.body: The back of the tongue blocks the mouth against the lowered velum. No /ɡ/ follows it in English.
ipa:ŋ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:ŋ.title: [ŋ] velar nasal

ipa:ŋ̍.body: The back of the tongue stays on the velum after the /k/ and hums the last syllable through the nose: the /n/ of “bacon” has taken the /k/'s place.
ipa:ŋ̍.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:ŋ̍.title: [ŋ̍] syllabic velar nasal

ipa:ɐ.body: A schwa with the jaw a little lower. espeak uses it for heavily reduced vowels. It counts as a weak vowel, like [ə].
ipa:ɐ.learnMoreLabel: See the change it belongs to
ipa:ɐ.title: [ɐ] near-open central vowel

ipa:ɑ.body: Tongue low and pulled back, so the pharynx narrows behind it; the lips stay unrounded.
ipa:ɑ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:ɑ.title: [ɑ] open back unrounded vowel

ipa:ɑɹ.body: Open back vowel that turns into an /ɹ/: the tongue rises and bunches without ever touching.
ipa:ɑɹ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:ɑɹ.title: [ɑɹ] r-coloured vowel

ipa:ɑː.body: Tongue low and pulled back, so the pharynx narrows behind it; the lips stay unrounded.
ipa:ɑː.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:ɑː.title: [ɑ] open back unrounded vowel

ipa:ɑːɹ.body: Open back vowel that turns into an /ɹ/: the tongue rises and bunches without ever touching.
ipa:ɑːɹ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:ɑːɹ.title: [ɑɹ] r-coloured vowel

ipa:ɒ.body: Low and back with a trace of rounding. American English usually merges it into /ɑ/.
ipa:ɒ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:ɒ.title: [ɒ] open back rounded vowel

ipa:ɔ.body: Low at the back with the lips slightly rounded. Many Americans no longer separate it from /ɑ/.
ipa:ɔ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:ɔ.title: [ɔ] open-mid back rounded vowel

ipa:ɔɪ.body: Starts back and rounded, then slides forward and up to /ɪ/: the longest trip in the vowel space.
ipa:ɔɪ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:ɔɪ.title: [ɔɪ] closing diphthong

ipa:ɔɹ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:ɔɹ.title: [ɔɹ] r-coloured vowel

ipa:ɔː.body: Low at the back with the lips slightly rounded. Many Americans no longer separate it from /ɑ/.
ipa:ɔː.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:ɔː.title: [ɔ] open-mid back rounded vowel

ipa:ɔːɹ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:ɔːɹ.title: [ɔɹ] r-coloured vowel

ipa:ə.body: The resting mouth, with voice: tongue in the middle, no effort anywhere. Every unstressed vowel in English drifts here. The most frequent vowel of spoken English: “about”, “banana”, and the weak forms of “to”, “of” and “a”.
ipa:ə.learnMoreLabel: See the change it belongs to
ipa:ə.title: [ə] mid central vowel (schwa)

ipa:əl.body: Schwa straight into a dark /l/: the tongue goes up to the ridge while the back stays low.
ipa:əl.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:əl.title: [əl] syllabic l

ipa:ɚ.body: Schwa plus /ɹ/ in one movement: the body of the tongue bunches towards the palate and the root pulls back. The -er of “letter”, and the weak form of “for” and “your”.
ipa:ɚ.learnMoreLabel: See the change it belongs to
ipa:ɚ.title: [ɚ] r-coloured mid central vowel

ipa:ɛ.body: Front of the tongue at mid height, jaw clearly more open than for /ɪ/.
ipa:ɛ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:ɛ.title: [ɛ] open-mid front unrounded vowel

ipa:ɛɹ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:ɛɹ.title: [ɛɹ] r-coloured vowel

ipa:ɜ.body: Central and mid, with no r-colouring. In American English it almost always turns up as /ɝ/.
ipa:ɜ.example: As in: nurse without the r
ipa:ɜ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:ɜ.title: [ɜ] open-mid central vowel

ipa:ɜː.body: Central and mid, with no r-colouring. In American English it almost always turns up as /ɝ/.
ipa:ɜː.example: As in: nurse without the r
ipa:ɜː.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:ɜː.title: [ɜ] open-mid central vowel

ipa:ɝ.body: The stressed /ɚ/: the same bunched tongue, held longer and louder.
ipa:ɝ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:ɝ.title: [ɝ] stressed r-coloured vowel

ipa:ɡ.body: The same back seal as /k/, voiced.
ipa:ɡ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:ɡ.title: [ɡ] voiced velar stop

ipa:ɡ̚.body: The /ɡ/ seal at the velum, voiced as it closes and never opened.
ipa:ɡ̚.example: As in: the -g of “big” in “big deal”
ipa:ɡ̚.learnMoreLabel: See the change it belongs to
ipa:ɡ̚.title: [ɡ̚] unreleased voiced velar stop

ipa:ɪ.body: Like /i/ but loose: the tongue drops a little and pulls back. Keeping it tense turns “sit” into “seat”.
ipa:ɪ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:ɪ.title: [ɪ] near-close near-front unrounded vowel

ipa:ɪɹ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:ɪɹ.title: [ɪɹ] r-coloured vowel

ipa:ɹ.body: Nothing touches anything: the body of the tongue bunches up towards the palate, the root pulls back and the lips round a little. Some speakers curl the tip up instead. Never a tap or a trill, unlike Spanish r.
ipa:ɹ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:ɹ.title: [ɹ] alveolar approximant

ipa:ɾ.body: The tip bounces off the ridge once, too briefly to build up any pressure. This is what American /t/ and /d/ become between vowels. You hear it in “water”, “better” and “get it”. It is the single r of Spanish “pero”: you can already say it.
ipa:ɾ.learnMoreLabel: See the change it belongs to
ipa:ɾ.title: [ɾ] alveolar tap

ipa:ɾ̃.body: The same single tap as /ɾ/, but the velum stays down from the /n/ before it, so the tap sounds through the nose. It is why “winter” can sound like “winner”. Heard in “winter”, “twenty” and “internet” said fast.
ipa:ɾ̃.learnMoreLabel: See the change it belongs to
ipa:ɾ̃.title: [ɾ̃] alveolar nasal tap

ipa:ʃ.body: The tongue pulls back a little from /s/ and the lips round: a deeper, darker hiss.
ipa:ʃ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:ʃ.title: [ʃ] voiceless postalveolar fricative

ipa:ʊ.body: High and back but loose, with only a hint of rounding.
ipa:ʊ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:ʊ.title: [ʊ] near-close near-back rounded vowel

ipa:ʊɹ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:ʊɹ.title: [ʊɹ] r-coloured vowel

ipa:ʌ.body: Tongue central and relaxed, jaw half open, lips doing nothing at all. The short “uh” of “cup”: not [æ] (cat) and not [ɑ] (father).
ipa:ʌ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:ʌ.title: [ʌ] open-mid back unrounded vowel

ipa:ʒ.body: The voiced twin of /ʃ/. It is what /z/ turns into before a /j/ (“as you” → aʒu).
ipa:ʒ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:ʒ.title: [ʒ] voiced postalveolar fricative

ipa:ʔ.body: The vocal folds close and cut the sound off. The mouth does nothing — that is why a glottalised /t/ looks like no /t/ at all. Heard as the t of “button” or “important”, like the catch in “uh-oh”.
ipa:ʔ.learnMoreLabel: See the change it belongs to
ipa:ʔ.title: [ʔ] glottal stop

ipa:θ.body: The tip of the tongue comes out between the teeth and the air passes over it. Many Spanish speakers say [s] or [t] here, but English keeps “think”, “sink” and “tink” apart.
ipa:θ.learnMoreLabel: See it in the IPA chart
ipa:θ.title: [θ] voiceless dental fricative

ipa:ᵻ.body: The unstressed /ɪ/: as high as /ɪ/ but pulled back towards the centre, halfway to schwa. It is what tells “roses” from “Rosa's”.
ipa:ᵻ.learnMoreLabel: See the change it belongs to
ipa:ᵻ.title: [ᵻ] near-close central unrounded vowel

linking.body: Two words joined without a pause. The end of one word runs into the start of the next.
linking.title: Linking

low-confidence.body: The recognizer found little or nothing here (silence, laughter, music, overlapping voices). Labels on this word may be wrong.
low-confidence.title: Low confidence

metric:deviate.body: Words where at least one sound was not the one the dictionary gives: changed, dropped or added. This is the headline of the research on spoken English: most words in real conversation do not sound like their dictionary form.
metric:deviate.example: water → wɔɾɚ (the t became a flap)
metric:deviate.title: Words that differ from the dictionary

metric:flapping.body: Where a t or d sits after a vowel and before an unstressed vowel, how often it became a flap [ɾ], a quick tap like the Spanish r in "pero". Only the places where flapping can happen are counted.
metric:flapping.title: Flapped t and d

metric:function_words.body: Of all the words, how many were small grammar words: to, of, and, the, can, you… They are usually unstressed and reduced, so a large part of what you hear is reduced by default.
metric:function_words.example: a cup of tea → ə kʌp ə ti
metric:function_words.title: Function words

metric:glottal_before_syllabic_n.body: A t before a syllabic n, as in "button" or "certain", said as a glottal stop. This is the usual American pronunciation of these words.
metric:glottal_before_syllabic_n.title: Glottal t before a syllabic n

metric:glottal_prevocalic.body: A t at the end of a word, before a word that starts with a vowel, said as a glottal stop [ʔ]: a short catch in the throat instead of a t. It is more common in younger speakers.
metric:glottal_prevocalic.title: Final t as a glottal stop

metric:labels_per_100_words.body: How often each phenomenon was found, scaled to 100 words, so recordings of different lengths can be compared.
metric:labels_per_100_words.title: Phenomena per 100 words

metric:low_confidence.body: Words where the recognizer heard almost nothing: silence, laughter or music over the voice. They are left out of the measures above.
metric:low_confidence.title: Low-confidence words

metric:schwa_share.body: Of all the vowels heard, how many were schwa [ə], the short, relaxed "uh" of unstressed syllables. It is the most frequent vowel of spoken English; Spanish has no vowel like it, so it is worth learning to hear.
metric:schwa_share.title: Schwa among the vowels

metric:segment_loss.body: Words where at least one whole sound disappeared, not just changed. When you listen, a missing sound is easy to take for a different word.
metric:segment_loss.example: next day → nɛks deɪ (the t is gone)
metric:segment_loss.title: Words that lose a sound

metric:syllable_loss.body: Words that came out with fewer syllables than the dictionary gives, usually because an unstressed vowel vanished. The word gets shorter than you expect.
metric:syllable_loss.title: Words that lose a syllable

metric:weak_forms.body: Of the function words, how many the recognizer heard in their weak form, with the vowel reduced or a sound dropped. The strong form appears mostly at the end of a phrase or when the word is stressed.
metric:weak_forms.example: to → tə, of → əv, and → ən
metric:weak_forms.title: Function words in their weak form

metric:weak_forms_variant.body: Only for the espeak engine: each function word is scored against its strong and weak pronunciations, and only the confident decisions are counted here.
metric:weak_forms_variant.title: Weak forms by form scoring

phenomenon.body: A regular change that happens when words are said in a stream, not one by one: a vowel weakens, a /t/ becomes a tap, two words link.
phenomenon.title: Connected-speech phenomenon

phone.body: One speech sound. Each IPA symbol stands for one phone: t, ɾ and ʔ are three different phones.
phone.title: Phone

prominence.body: How much a word stands out: higher pitch, louder, longer. English makes content words (nouns, verbs, adjectives) prominent and reduces grammar words.
prominence.title: Prominence

recognize-only.body: Learn to hear it, but you do not need to say it: it is casual, regional or socially marked, and it can sound forced from a learner.
recognize-only.title: Recognize only

register.body: How widely a change is used: universal (every speaker, every situation), casual (relaxed speech) or marked (a region or group).
register.title: Register

rhythm.body: How regular the syllables are. English stretches stressed syllables and squeezes the rest; Spanish keeps them more even. Measured here from the spacing of syllables, so treat it as a rough guide.
rhythm.title: Rhythm (approximate)

safe-to-produce.body: Native speakers use this change in every register, and a learner sounds natural using it too. Copy it.
safe-to-produce.title: Safe to produce

schwa.body: The short, relaxed vowel [ə], as in the first sound of about. It is the most frequent vowel in spoken English: unstressed vowels turn into it.
schwa.title: Schwa

semitone.body: A step of pitch, the same for every voice. Measuring in semitones lets a deep voice and a high voice be compared.
semitone.title: Semitone

separation.body: Before analyzing, the voices are separated from music and sound effects, so the recognizer hears speech only. You can play either the original mix or the dialogue alone.
separation.title: Dialogue separation

strong-form.body: The full pronunciation of a grammar word. It appears at the end of a phrase, under emphasis, or when quoted: “Yes, I can.”
strong-form.title: Strong form

uptalk.body: A statement that ends with a rise, as if it were a question. Common in younger American speakers; you will hear it, but you do not need to produce it.
uptalk.title: Uptalk

weak-form.body: Small grammar words (to, of, and, can, you…) have a strong form and a weak form. In normal speech the weak one, usually with a schwa [ə], is the default.
weak-form.title: Weak form

what-was-said.body: The sounds the recognizer actually heard in this recording. Written between square brackets: […].
what-was-said.title: What was said

allophoneRows.detail: the closure is made but never opened
allophoneRows.label: Unreleased stop

allophoneRows.detail: one very quick touch of the tongue
allophoneRows.label: Tap

allophoneRows.detail: the throat closes for an instant
allophoneRows.label: Glottal stop

consonantRows.detail: the air is stopped completely, then released
consonantRows.label: Stop

consonantRows.detail: a stop that opens into a hiss
consonantRows.label: Affricate

consonantRows.detail: the air hisses through a narrow gap
consonantRows.label: Fricative

consonantRows.detail: the air goes out through the nose
consonantRows.label: Nasal

consonantRows.detail: the tongue or lips come close without touching
consonantRows.label: Approximant

consonantRows.detail: the air flows around the sides of the tongue
consonantRows.label: Lateral

glidingGroups.detail: the tongue glides from one vowel to another
glidingGroups.label: Diphthongs

glidingGroups.detail: a vowel that ends with the tongue in the r position
glidingGroups.label: Vowels with r

glidingGroups.detail: heard in accents without r, and in a few words
glidingGroups.label: Non-rhotic glides

vowelRows.detail: the relaxed middle of the mouth
vowelRows.label: Mid

contraction_lex.listenFor: Two words fuse into one fixed form: “going to” → “gonna”, “want to” → “wanna”, “got to” → “gotta”, “let me” → “lemme”.
contraction_lex.note: “gonna” is only for the future before a verb (I'm gonna leave), never for movement (not “I'm gonna the store”). “wanna” only when want and to are side by side: “Who do you wanna win?” is wrong.

elision_syllable.listenFor: A whole unstressed syllable is skipped, so the word has one beat less: “probably” → “prob-ly”, “camera” → “cam-ra”, “family” → “fam-ly”.

flapping.listenFor: A t or d between vowels becomes one very quick tap of the tongue: “water” sounds like “wadder”, “get it” like “geddit”.
flapping.note: Not before a stressed syllable: “attack” and “return” keep a full t.
flapping.spanishTip: The flap is the single r of Spanish “pero”. You already have this sound: use it for the t of “water”, “better” or “a lot of”.

function_elision.listenFor: A small function word keeps almost nothing: “of” → [ə] (“cup of tea” → “cuppa tea”), “them” → [əm] (“tell 'em”).

glottalization.listenFor: The t is replaced by a catch in the throat, as in “uh-oh”: “button” → “bu'n”, “important” → “impor'nt”.

h_dropping.listenFor: In unstressed he, him, his, her and have the h disappears: “tell him” → “tell-im”, “give her” → “giver”.
h_dropping.note: Never at the start of a sentence: “He is here” keeps its h.

linking.listenFor: There is no pause between the words: a final consonant moves onto the next vowel (“pick it up” → “pi-ki-dup”), an r joins the next word (“far away”), or a w or y glide appears between two vowels (“go on” → “go-won”).
linking.note: American English never adds an r that is not written (“idea-r-is” is British).

monophthongization.listenFor: A two-part vowel stays on its first part: “my” sounds like “ma”, “time” like “tahm”.

nt_reduction.listenFor: The t after n disappears or becomes a nasal tap: “twenty” → “twenny”, “winter” → almost “winner”, “internet” → “innernet”.
nt_reduction.note: Very American but variable: “winter” and “winner” often stay slightly different.

palatalization.listenFor: A final t, d, s or z melts into a following “you”: “did you” → “didja”, “got you” → “gotcha”, “miss you” → “mishu”.

place_assimilation.listenFor: A final n, t or d takes the place of the next sound: “ten bucks” → “tem bucks”, “in case” → “ing case”, “good boy” → “goob boy”.
place_assimilation.note: It happens by itself in fast speech; forcing it sounds odd. Learn to hear it.

t_deletion.listenFor: When a word ends in a group of consonants, the t or d is skipped before the next consonant: “next day” → “nex' day”, “old man” → “ol' man”.

t_unreleased.listenFor: At the end of a word the tongue closes for t, but no puff of air follows: “that one” sounds like “tha' one”, with a tiny silence where the t should be.

th_stopping.listenFor: th is said as a plain d or t: “that” → “dat”, “thing” → “ting”.
th_stopping.spanishTip: Many Spanish speakers already mix [ð] with [d]. Here it is a regional native feature to recognize — keep practising [θ] and [ð] in your own speech.

vowel_reduction.listenFor: Unstressed syllables get short and quiet, and their vowel becomes a neutral “uh” [ə]. Listen for the small words — to, of, a, can, for — that almost vanish between the stressed ones.
vowel_reduction.note: “can” reduces to [kən], but “can't” keeps its full [æ]: the vowel, not the t, tells them apart.
vowel_reduction.spanishTip: Spanish gives every vowel its full value. Saying ba-NA-na with three clear a's instead of [bəˈnænə] is the most audible accent marker — and it also makes the reduced word hard to recognize.

word_elision.listenFor: The word is so short and quiet that no sound was found for it — usually a small function word in fast speech, or a word buried under laughter or music.
word_elision.note: Read this label with caution: it can also be a gap in the recognition.

phones.cue: Both lips seal, the pressure builds up behind them, and the release is a puff of air.
phones.name: voiceless bilabial stop

phones.cue: The same seal as /p/, but the vocal folds are already vibrating when it opens.
phones.name: voiced bilabial stop

phones.cue: The tip of the tongue seals against the ridge behind the upper teeth.
phones.name: voiceless alveolar stop

phones.cue: The same seal as /t/, with the voice running through it.
phones.name: voiced alveolar stop

phones.cue: The back of the tongue rises and seals against the soft palate.
phones.name: voiceless velar stop

phones.cue: The same back seal as /k/, voiced.
phones.name: voiced velar stop

phones.cue: The vocal folds close and cut the sound off. The mouth does nothing — that is why a glottalised /t/ looks like no /t/ at all.
phones.name: glottal stop

phones.cue: The lips seal as for /p/ and stay sealed: no puff of air, the next sound starts from behind closed lips.
phones.name: unreleased voiceless bilabial stop

phones.cue: The /b/ seal held shut and never opened; the voice fades away inside the closure.
phones.name: unreleased voiced bilabial stop

phones.cue: The tip seals on the ridge and simply stays there: no burst. American English does this to most final /t/s — the /t/ is in the mouth, not in the ear.
phones.name: unreleased voiceless alveolar stop

phones.cue: The /d/ seal held with no release; the voicing dies away inside the closure.
phones.name: unreleased voiced alveolar stop

phones.cue: The back of the tongue seals against the velum and stays there; the release never comes.
phones.name: unreleased voiceless velar stop

phones.cue: The /ɡ/ seal at the velum, voiced as it closes and never opened.
phones.name: unreleased voiced velar stop

phones.cue: Lips closed and the velum drops: the whole airstream leaves through the nose.
phones.name: bilabial nasal

phones.cue: Tongue tip on the ridge and velum down: the mouth is blocked, the nose is not.
phones.name: alveolar nasal

phones.cue: The back of the tongue blocks the mouth against the lowered velum. No /ɡ/ follows it in English.
phones.name: velar nasal

phones.cue: An /n/ that carries the syllable by itself: the tongue never leaves the ridge, and there is no vowel before it.
phones.name: syllabic alveolar nasal

phones.cue: An /m/ that is the whole syllable: the lips stay closed and the voice hums through the nose with no vowel before it.
phones.name: syllabic bilabial nasal

phones.cue: The back of the tongue stays on the velum after the /k/ and hums the last syllable through the nose: the /n/ of “bacon” has taken the /k/'s place.
phones.name: syllabic velar nasal

phones.cue: The lower lip touches the upper teeth and the air hisses between them. The lips never meet each other.
phones.name: voiceless labiodental fricative

phones.cue: Like /f/, with voice. Watch the lip against the teeth: a /b/ closes both lips instead.
phones.name: voiced labiodental fricative

phones.cue: The tip of the tongue comes out between the teeth and the air passes over it.
phones.name: voiceless dental fricative

phones.cue: The same tongue between the teeth as /θ/, with the voice on.
phones.name: voiced dental fricative

phones.cue: A narrow groove between the tip of the tongue and the ridge; the air whistles through it.
phones.name: voiceless alveolar fricative

phones.cue: The same groove as /s/, with the vocal folds vibrating.
phones.name: voiced alveolar fricative

phones.cue: The tongue pulls back a little from /s/ and the lips round: a deeper, darker hiss.
phones.name: voiceless postalveolar fricative

phones.cue: The voiced twin of /ʃ/. It is what /z/ turns into before a /j/ (“as you” → aʒu).
phones.name: voiced postalveolar fricative

phones.cue: Nothing blocks the mouth: the noise is made at the vocal folds while the tongue is already shaped for the vowel that follows.
phones.name: voiceless glottal fricative

phones.cue: A stop that does not open straight up: it releases into the hiss of /ʃ/.
phones.name: voiceless postalveolar affricate

phones.cue: The voiced version: closure and then /ʒ/. It is what /d/ becomes before a /j/ (“did you” → dɪdʒu).
phones.name: voiced postalveolar affricate

phones.cue: The tip bounces off the ridge once, too briefly to build up any pressure. This is what American /t/ and /d/ become between vowels.
phones.name: alveolar tap

phones.cue: The same single tap as /ɾ/, but the velum stays down from the /n/ before it, so the tap sounds through the nose. It is why “winter” can sound like “winner”.
phones.name: alveolar nasal tap

phones.cue: The tip touches the ridge but the sides of the tongue stay clear: the air leaves around them. At the end of a syllable the back rises too — that is the “dark” l.
phones.name: alveolar lateral approximant

phones.cue: A dark /l/ that is the whole syllable: no vowel comes before it, the tongue goes straight to the ridge.
phones.name: syllabic alveolar lateral

phones.cue: Nothing touches anything: the body of the tongue bunches up towards the palate, the root pulls back and the lips round a little. Some speakers curl the tip up instead.
phones.name: alveolar approximant

phones.cue: The tongue starts as high and as front as an /i/ and immediately slides off it.
phones.name: palatal approximant

phones.cue: Two narrowings at once: the lips round hard and the back of the tongue rises towards the velum.
phones.name: labial-velar approximant

phones.cue: The tongue is as high and as far forward as it goes without hissing; the lips are spread.
phones.name: close front unrounded vowel

phones.cue: Like /i/ but loose: the tongue drops a little and pulls back. Keeping it tense turns “sit” into “seat”.
phones.name: near-close near-front unrounded vowel

phones.cue: Front of the tongue at mid height, jaw clearly more open than for /ɪ/.
phones.name: open-mid front unrounded vowel

phones.cue: The front of the tongue stays forward while the jaw drops wide open. It is the widest front vowel English has.
phones.name: near-open front unrounded vowel

phones.cue: Tongue low and pulled back, so the pharynx narrows behind it; the lips stay unrounded.
phones.name: open back unrounded vowel

phones.cue: Low and back with a trace of rounding. American English usually merges it into /ɑ/.
phones.name: open back rounded vowel

phones.cue: Tongue central and relaxed, jaw half open, lips doing nothing at all.
phones.name: open-mid back unrounded vowel

phones.cue: Low at the back with the lips slightly rounded. Many Americans no longer separate it from /ɑ/.
phones.name: open-mid back rounded vowel

phones.cue: High and back but loose, with only a hint of rounding.
phones.name: near-close near-back rounded vowel

phones.cue: The back of the tongue rises towards the velum while the lips round and push forward.
phones.name: close back rounded vowel

phones.cue: The resting mouth, with voice: tongue in the middle, no effort anywhere. Every unstressed vowel in English drifts here.
phones.name: mid central vowel (schwa)

phones.cue: A schwa with the jaw a little lower. espeak uses it for heavily reduced vowels.
phones.name: near-open central vowel

phones.cue: The unstressed /ɪ/: as high as /ɪ/ but pulled back towards the centre, halfway to schwa. It is what tells “roses” from “Rosa's”.
phones.name: near-close central unrounded vowel

phones.cue: Schwa plus /ɹ/ in one movement: the body of the tongue bunches towards the palate and the root pulls back.
phones.name: r-coloured mid central vowel

phones.cue: The stressed /ɚ/: the same bunched tongue, held longer and louder.
phones.name: stressed r-coloured vowel

phones.cue: Central and mid, with no r-colouring. In American English it almost always turns up as /ɝ/.
phones.name: open-mid central vowel

phones.cue: Starts near /ɛ/ and closes upwards to /ɪ/. Stopping at the start is the commonest way to make it sound foreign.
phones.name: closing diphthong

phones.cue: Starts mid-back with the lips already rounded and closes towards /ʊ/.
phones.name: closing diphthong

phones.cue: The jaw starts wide open with the tongue low, then everything closes up to /ɪ/.
phones.name: closing diphthong

phones.cue: Starts low, then the tongue pulls back and the lips round towards /ʊ/.
phones.name: closing diphthong

phones.cue: Starts back and rounded, then slides forward and up to /ɪ/: the longest trip in the vowel space.
phones.name: closing diphthong

phones.cue: Open back vowel that turns into an /ɹ/: the tongue rises and bunches without ever touching.
phones.name: r-coloured vowel

phones.cue: Rounded back vowel closing into /ɹ/.
phones.name: r-coloured vowel

phones.cue: Like “north” but starting higher; most Americans no longer keep the two apart.
phones.name: r-coloured vowel

phones.cue: /ɪ/ falling back into the bunched /ɹ/.
phones.name: r-coloured vowel

phones.cue: /ɛ/ falling back into the bunched /ɹ/.
phones.name: r-coloured vowel

phones.cue: /ʊ/ unrounding as it turns into /ɹ/.
phones.name: r-coloured vowel

phones.cue: Three targets without a pause: open, then /ɪ/, then r-coloured.
phones.name: triphthong

phones.cue: Like “fire” but ending in a plain schwa, with no r-colouring.
phones.name: triphthong

phones.cue: /i/ relaxing back into schwa.
phones.name: centring diphthong

phones.cue: Mid front vowel relaxing back into schwa.
phones.name: centring diphthong

phones.cue: Schwa straight into a dark /l/: the tongue goes up to the ridge while the back stays low.
phones.name: syllabic l

phones.cue: /j/ then /u/: the tongue starts against the palate and slides back while the lips round.
phones.name: rising diphthong
